claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers is governed by interface-mediated dislocation nucleation and accumulation.
Severe lattice distortion and short-range order at nanoscale FCC/BCC interfaces modulate local dislocation behavior.
The starting coating consists of alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers with distinct nanoscale interfaces.
The starting interfaces possess inherent lattice distortions and short-range chemical order.
A suitable stress-temperature regime can permit time-dependent plasticity while preventing dislocation climb, diffusion-dominated creep, and phase transformations.
Lattice misfit, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order at FCC/BCC interfaces generate localized stress concentrations.
The localized interfacial stress concentrations make the interfaces preferential sites for dislocation nucleation and accumulation.
Sustained loading concentrates stress at the interfaces and promotes dislocation nucleation.
Lattice distortion and short-range order hinder dislocation recovery and transmission across the interfaces.
Hindered recovery and transmission cause interfacial dislocation pile-ups that initially pin deformation.
Once the interfacial barriers are overwhelmed, localized interface sliding is triggered.
Localized interface sliding accelerates plastic deformation.
FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers will initially have a lower creep strain rate than conventional multilayers or homogeneous alloys because of interfacial dislocation pinning.
The initial low-rate regime will be followed by localized acceleration of plastic deformation as dislocation pile-ups develop.
Conventional multilayers or homogeneous high-entropy alloys exhibit more uniform dislocation-mediated plasticity under similar loading conditions.

The proposed behavior applies only while the nanoscale multilayer architecture remains intact and interfacial dislocation activity dominates over diffusion, phase transformation, and catastrophic interface degradation.
Variations in local chemistry may alter the onset of accelerated creep.
